claim: The epidermis is a multilayered epithelium that surrounds and protects the vertebrate body.
source: The epidermis, a multilayered epithelium, surrounds and protects the vertebrate body.
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge about the epidermis.

claim: The epidermis develops from a bilayered epithelium formed of the outer periderm and underlying basal epidermis.
source: It develops from a bilayered epithelium formed of the outer periderm and underlying basal epidermis.
evidence: This is a statement of established biological knowledge about epidermis development.

claim: Both the periderm and the basal epidermis exhibit polarised distribution of adherens junctions in zebrafish.
source: We show that both the periderm and the basal epidermis exhibit polarised distribution of adherens junctions in zebrafish.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: aPKC maintains the robustness of polarisation of E-cadherin in the periderm.
source: aPKC, an apical polarity regulator, maintains the robustness of polarisation of E-cadherin- an adherens junction component- in the periderm.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from has/apkc mutant analysis.

claim: E-cadherin in one layer controls the localisation of E-cadherin in the second layer in a layer non-autonomous manner.
source: E-cadherin in one layer controls the localisation of E-cadherin in the second layer in a layer non-autonomous manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by clonal knockdown experiments.

claim: E-cadherin controls the localisation and levels of Lgl in a layer autonomous as well as non-autonomous manner.
source: Importantly, E-cadherin controls the localisation and levels of Lgl, a basolateral polarity regulator, in a layer autonomous as well non-autonomous manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by clonal knockdown experiments.

claim: Periderm formation from the enveloping layer precedes the formation of the basal epidermis.
source: Since periderm formation from the enveloping layer precedes the formation of the basal epidermis, our analyses suggest that peridermal polarity, initiated by aPKC, is transduced in a stepwise manner by E-cadherin to the basal layer.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of zebrafish epidermis development.

claim: Peridermal polarity, initiated by aPKC, is transduced in a stepwise manner by E-cadherin to the basal layer.
source: Since periderm formation from the enveloping layer precedes the formation of the basal epidermis, our analyses suggest that peridermal polarity, initiated by aPKC, is transduced in a stepwise manner by E-cadherin to the basal layer.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings and developmental timing.

claim: The mammalian epidermis begins as a single layer during embryogenesis.
source: During embryogenesis, the mammalian epidermis begins as a single layer, becomes bilayered and eventually develops into a multi-layered and keratinised tissue (Blanpain and Fuchs, 2009; Evans and Rutter, 1986; Koster and Roop, 2007; M'Boneko and Merker, 1988; Nakamura and Yasuda, 1979; Saathoff et al., 2004; Smart, 1970).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The mammalian epidermis becomes bilayered and eventually develops into a multi-layered and keratinised tissue.
source: During embryogenesis, the mammalian epidermis begins as a single layer, becomes bilayered and eventually develops into a multi-layered and keratinised tissue (Blanpain and Fuchs, 2009; Evans and Rutter, 1986; Koster and Roop, 2007; M'Boneko and Merker, 1988; Nakamura and Yasuda, 1979; Saathoff et al., 2004; Smart, 1970).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: In zebrafish, the early bilayered epidermis is formed of an outer periderm and inner basal epidermis.
source: In zebrafish, the early bilayered epidermis is formed of an outer periderm, which differentiates from the enveloping layer (EVL), and inner basal epidermis that develops from the non-neuralised ectoderm (Bakkers et al., 2002; Chang and Hwang, 2011; Kimmel et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The periderm differentiates from the enveloping layer (EVL).
source: In zebrafish, the early bilayered epidermis is formed of an outer periderm, which differentiates from the enveloping layer (EVL), and inner basal epidermis that develops from the non-neuralised ectoderm (Bakkers et al., 2002; Chang and Hwang, 2011; Kimmel et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The basal epidermis develops from the non-neuralised ectoderm.
source: In zebrafish, the early bilayered epidermis is formed of an outer periderm, which differentiates from the enveloping layer (EVL), and inner basal epidermis that develops from the non-neuralised ectoderm (Bakkers et al., 2002; Chang and Hwang, 2011; Kimmel et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The bilayered epithelium in zebrafish is present in the embryonic and larval stages but becomes multi-layered during metamorphosis.
source: This bilayered epithelium is present in the embryonic and larval stages but becomes multi-layered during metamorphosis (Chang and Hwang, 2011; Le Guellec et al., 2004; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The epidermis is polarised at the tissue level.
source: Several lines of evidence indicate that the epidermis is polarised at the tissue level (Brandner et al., 2010; Getsios et al., 2004; Muroyama and Lechler, 2012; Watt, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Tight junction components such as Cldn-1, ZO-1 and Occludin are localised differentially across layers in the mammalian epidermis.
source: Tight junction components such as Cldn-1, ZO-1 and Occludin are localised differentially across layers in the mammalian epidermis (Brandner, 2009; Brandner et al., 2002; Kirschner and Brandner, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Desmosomal cadherins, plakophillins, envoplakin and periplakin show differentiation dependent changes in expression levels across layers in the epidermis.
source: Desmosomal cadherins, plakophillins, envoplakin and periplakin show differentiation dependent changes in expression levels across layers in the epidermis (Getsios et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Hemidesmosomes mediating the cell-matrix adhesions form only in the basal domain of basal epidermal cells.
source: Besides, hemidesmosomes mediating the cell-matrix adhesions form only in the basal domain of basal epidermal cells (Hieda et al., 1992; Owaribe et al., 1990; Sonawane et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A simple epithelium has a well-defined apicobasal polarity.
source: A simple epithelium has a well-defined apicobasal polarity; the side that faces the lumen or external environment is defined as the apical domain and the side that is in contact with the basement membrane and neighbouring cells is called the basolateral domain (Rodriguez-Boulan and Macara, 2014; Tepass, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In vertebrates, the tight junctions demarcate the apical domain and separate the apical domain from the basolateral domain.
source: In vertebrates, the tight junctions demarcate the apical domain and thus separate the apical domain from the basolateral domain (Rodriguez-Boulan and Macara, 2014; Tepass, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Simple epithelia possess an apical zonula adherens, a tight belt of cadherin mediated adherens junctions.
source: In addition, simple epithelia possess an apical zonula adherens, a tight belt of cadherin mediated adherens junctions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about simple epithelia.

claim: The formation and proper apical localisation of tight and adherens junctions marks an important step in polarisation of the epithelial sheet.
source: The formation and proper apical localisation of tight and adherens junctions marks an important step in polarisation of the epithelial sheet and is tightly controlled by the epithelial polarity pathways (Laprise and Tepass, 2011; Rodriguez-Boulan and Macara, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: At least four modules or pathways are important for establishment and maintenance of apicobasal polarity in the simple epithelia.
source: At least four modules or pathways are important for establishment and maintenance of apicobasal polarity in the simple epithelia.
evidence: This is established knowledge about epithelial polarity.

claim: aPKC-Par3-Par6 and Crb-Sdt-Patj control the apical polarity.
source: Amongst these aPKC-Par3-Par6, Crb-Sdt-Patj control the apical polarity and Lgl-Dlg-Scrb, Yurt-Cora-Nrx IV-Na+K+ATPase regulate the basolateral polarity (Bilder et al., 2000; Bilder and Perrimon, 2000; Kemphues et al., 1988; Laprise et al., 2009; Tepass et al., 1990; Wodarz et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Lgl-Dlg-Scrb and Yurt-Cora-Nrx IV-Na+K+ATPase regulate the basolateral polarity.
source: Amongst these aPKC-Par3-Par6, Crb-Sdt-Patj control the apical polarity and Lgl-Dlg-Scrb, Yurt-Cora-Nrx IV-Na+K+ATPase regulate the basolateral polarity (Bilder et al., 2000; Bilder and Perrimon, 2000; Kemphues et al., 1988; Laprise et al., 2009; Tepass et al., 1990; Wodarz et al., 1995).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The loss of apkc function results in the disruption of adherens junctions in Drosophila neuroectoderm.
source: The loss of apkc function results in the disruption of adherens junctions in Drosophila neuroectoderm (Wodarz et al., 2000), the intestine and retinae of zebrafish (Horne-Badovinac et al., 2001), and in the neuroepithelium of mice (Imai et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The loss of apkc function results in the disruption of adherens junctions in the intestine and retinae of zebrafish.
source: The loss of apkc function results in the disruption of adherens junctions in Drosophila neuroectoderm (Wodarz et al., 2000), the intestine and retinae of zebrafish (Horne-Badovinac et al., 2001), and in the neuroepithelium of mice (Imai et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The loss of apkc function results in the disruption of adherens junctions in the neuroepithelium of mice.
source: The loss of apkc function results in the disruption of adherens junctions in Drosophila neuroectoderm (Wodarz et al., 2000), the intestine and retinae of zebrafish (Horne-Badovinac et al., 2001), and in the neuroepithelium of mice (Imai et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The absence of lgl function results in mislocalisation of the adherens junctions and expansion of apical domain in multiple Drosophila epithelial tissues.
source: The absence of lgl function results in mislocalisation of the adherens junctions and expansion of apical domain in multiple Drosophila epithelial tissues (Bilder et al., 2000; Tanentzapf and Tepass, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Formation and localisation of tight junctions is regulated by cell polarity regulators apkc and lgl.
source: Similar to adherens junctions, formation and localisation of tight junctions is also shown to be regulated by cell polarity regulators apkc and lgl (Chalmers et al., 2005; Iden et al., 2012; Yamanaka et al., 2006; Yamanaka et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In mouse epidermis, aPKC regulates the cell division plane and maintains the stem cells in a quiescent stage in the hair follicles.
source: In mouse epidermis, aPKC regulates the cell division plane and maintains the stem cells in a quiescent stage in the hair follicles (Helfrich et al., 2007; Niessen et al., 2013; Osada et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The aPKC function is required to build trans epithelial resistance in the basal keratinocytes cell culture.
source: The aPKC function is also required to build trans epithelial resistance in the basal keratinocytes cell culture (Helfrich et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In the embryonic epidermis, heart and soul (has)/apkc λ/í functions to control the elongation of microridges, actin based apical projections on the zebrafish peridermal cells.
source: In the embryonic epidermis, heart and soul (has)/apkc λ/í functions to control the elongation of microridges, actin based apical projections on the zebrafish peridermal cells (Raman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: penner/lgl2 function is essential for the formation of hemidesmosomes in the basal epidermis.
source: Amongst the basolateral components, penner/lgl2 function is essential for the formation of hemidesmosomes in the basal epidermis and to promote the elongation of microridges in the periderm in zebrafish (Raman et al., 2016; Sonawane et al., 2005; Sonawane et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: penner/lgl2 function promotes the elongation of microridges in the periderm in zebrafish.
source: Amongst the basolateral components, penner/lgl2 function is essential for the formation of hemidesmosomes in the basal epidermis and to promote the elongation of microridges in the periderm in zebrafish (Raman et al., 2016; Sonawane et al., 2005; Sonawane et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: psoriasis/atp1b1a regulates localisation of Lgl as well as E-cadherin and functions as a cell non-autonomous tumour suppressor in hypotonic conditions.
source: Furthermore, psoriasis/atp1b1a - encoding a subunit of Na+K+ATPase – regulates localisation of Lgl as well as E-cadherin and functions as a cell non-autonomous tumour suppressor in hypotonic conditions (Hatzold et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Adherens junctions contribute towards the polarisation of simple epithelia.
source: Adherens junctions contribute towards the polarisation of simple epithelia.
evidence: This is established knowledge about epithelial polarity.

claim: The loss of shotgun/de-cadherin and armadillo/β-catenin function is known to perturb the polarity and architecture of epithelial tissues in Drosophila.
source: The loss of shotgun/de-cadherin and armadillo/β-catenin function is known to perturb the polarity and architecture of epithelial tissues in Drosophila (Müller and Wieschaus, 1996; Tanentzapf et al., 2000; Tepass et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In mouse, epidermis-specific E-cadherin knockout shows mislocalisation of aPKC and Cdc42.
source: In mouse, epidermis- specific E-cadherin knockout shows mislocalisation of aPKC and Cdc42 (Tunggal et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: E-cadherin is required for the formation of tight junctions in the epidermis of mouse and zebrafish.
source: Moreover, E-cadherin is also required for the formation of tight junctions and regulation of hemidesmosome formation in the epidermis of mouse and zebrafish, respectively (Rübsam et al., 2017; Sonawane et al., 2009; Tunggal et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: E-cadherin is required for regulation of hemidesmosome formation in the epidermis of zebrafish.
source: Moreover, E-cadherin is also required for the formation of tight junctions and regulation of hemidesmosome formation in the epidermis of mouse and zebrafish, respectively (Rübsam et al., 2017; Sonawane et al., 2009; Tunggal et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: E-cadherin localisation increases gradually along the apicobasal axis of the peridermal cells at 48 hours post-fertilisation.
source: Analysis of successive confocal slices in z-stacks and immuno-histological sections revealed that the localisation of E-cadherin increases gradually along the apicobasal axis of the peridermal cells at 48 hours post-fertilisation (hpf; Figure 1A1, B1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: E-cadherin colocalised with Lgl, both in the periderm as well as in the basal epidermis.
source: Immunolocalisation analyses by confocal microscopy as well as histology revealed that E-cadherin colocalised with Lgl, both in the periderm as well as in the basal epidermis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mean E-cadherin levels increase gradually from the apical to the basal domain, plateauing at the basal domain of the peridermal cells, at all stages analysed between 24 to 72hpf.
source: This analysis revealed that the mean E-cadherin levels increase gradually from the apical to the basal domain, plateauing at the basal domain of the peridermal cells, at all stages analysed between 24 to 72hpf.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of experimental data.

claim: In the basal epidermis, E-cadherin levels were found to be higher at the apical domain and decreased gradually towards the basal domain.
source: In the basal epidermis, this distribution is reversed. E-cadherin levels were found to be higher at the apical domain and decreased gradually towards the basal domain (Figure 1 A2, B2, B5, C2; Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The mean E-cadherin intensity at each z-level increased in both the periderm and basal epidermis during development.
source: During development, the mean E-cadherin intensity at each z-level increased in both the periderm and basal epidermis (Figure 1 C1, C2; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: β-catenin shows a similar trend to E-cadherin in the periderm and basal epidermis.
source: A similar trend was observed for β-catenin, another component associated with the adherens junctions, in the periderm and basal epidermis (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The maximum levels of E-cadherin and β-catenin are present at the interface of both the layers.
source: Thus, the maximum levels of E-cadherin and β-catenin are present at the interface of both the layers.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the polarised distribution data.

claim: There is a significant increase in the membrane localisation of E-cadherin and β-catenin during development, especially between 48hpf to 72hpf.
source: Besides, there is a significant increase in the membrane localisation of E-cadherin and β-catenin during development, especially between 48hpf to 72hpf, suggesting an increase in the formation of adherens junctions during epidermis development.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing temporal changes.

claim: aPKC localises to the apical domain of the periderm.
source: While aPKC localises to the apical domain of the periderm, Lgl is localised to the basolateral domain of the peridermal cells and to the apicolateral domain of the basal epidermal cells (Figure 1 A1, B1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Raman et al. (2016); Sonawane et al. (2009)).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations.

claim: Lgl is localised to the basolateral domain of the peridermal cells and to the apicolateral domain of the basal epidermal cells.
source: While aPKC localises to the apical domain of the periderm, Lgl is localised to the basolateral domain of the peridermal cells and to the apicolateral domain of the basal epidermal cells (Figure 1 A1, B1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Raman et al. (2016); Sonawane et al. (2009)).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citations.

claim: A decrease in E-cadherin levels was observed in the periderm as well as in the basal epidermis of has/apkc mutant embryos at 48hpf.
source: We observed a decrease in E-cadherin levels in the periderm as well as in the basal epidermis of has/apkc mutant embryos at 48hpf (Figure 2 A1, B1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: has/apkc mutants had significantly higher number of taller peridermal cells as compared to wild-type siblings.
source: On comparing the cell morphology between has/apkc mutants and wild-type siblings, we found that mutants had significantly higher number of taller peridermal cells as compared to the siblings (Figure 2 A2, Mann Whitney U test, p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The apical perimeter of the mutant peridermal cells was smaller than that of siblings.
source: The apical perimeter of the mutant peridermal cells was also smaller than that of siblings (Figure 2 A3, Mann Whitney U test, p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: Irrespective of the cell height, mutant cells are more columnar than the sibling cells.
source: These data suggest that, irrespective of the cell height, mutant cells are more columnar than the sibling cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the apical perimeter data.

claim: There was no significant effect on the morphology of the basal epidermal cells in has/apkc mutant embryos as compared to the siblings.
source: In contrast, there was no significant effect on the morphology of the basal epidermal cells in has/apkc mutant embryos as compared to the siblings (Figure 2 B2, B3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Sibling peridermal cells show a noisy but gradual increase in E-cadherin intensity along the apico-basal axis.
source: We observed that, while sibling peridermal cells show a noisy but gradual increase in E-cadherin intensity along the apico-basal axis, the mutant peridermal cells exhibit increased noise and reduced robustness in polarised E-cadherin distribution (Figure 2 A4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The mutant peridermal cells exhibit increased noise and reduced robustness in polarised E-cadherin distribution.
source: We observed that, while sibling peridermal cells show a noisy but gradual increase in E-cadherin intensity along the apico-basal axis, the mutant peridermal cells exhibit increased noise and reduced robustness in polarised E-cadherin distribution (Figure 2 A4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Analysis on the basal epidermal cells did not show any obvious effects on the polarised distribution of E-cadherin in the has/apkc mutant embryos.
source: Similar analysis on the basal epidermal cells did not show any obvious effects on the polarised distribution of E-cadherin in the has/apkc mutant embryos (Figure 2 B4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The noise index was 24% for has/apkc mutant as compared to 8% for the siblings.
source: The noise index (abnormal cells*100/total cells) thus estimated was 24% for has/apkc mutant as compared to 8% for the siblings (Figure 2 A5).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the periderm of has/apkc mutants, irrespective of the cell heights, a decrease in the robustness of polarisation and an increase in noise index was observed.
source: Interestingly, in the periderm of has/apkc mutants, irrespective of the cell heights, a decrease in the robustness of polarisation and an increase in noise index was observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, C3, D2, D3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The effect on E-cadherin polarisation in has/apkc mutant embryos is independent of the cell heights.
source: These data suggest that the effect on E-cadherin polarisation in has/apkc mutant embryos is independent of the cell heights.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the height-stratified analysis.

claim: In the absence of has/apkc function, peridermal cells show a decrease in membrane localisation of E-cadherin-mCherry, reduction in the robustness of E-cadherin polarisation and increase in the noise index as compared to WT siblings.
source: This analysis corroborated the findings that in the absence of has/apkc function, peridermal cells show a decrease in membrane localisation of E-cadherin-mCherry, reduction in the robustness of E-cadherin polarisation and increase in the noise index as compared to WT siblings (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,D,E).
evidence: This is supported by live imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Injection of e-cadherin-mCherry mRNA specifically rescued the cell-height phenotype in the periderm of has/apkc mutants over the control injections of CAAX-mCherry mRNA.
source: Interestingly, injection of e-cadherin-mCherry mRNA, which presumably increases the total pool of E-cadherin (endogenous + exogenous), specifically rescued the cell-height phenotype in the periderm of has/apkc mutants over the control injections of CAAX-mCherry mRNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B, Kruskal Wallis test with Dunn's post hoc test; significance values in Figure 2—figure supplement 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Exogenously added E-cadherin failed to rescue the smaller apical perimeter of the mutant peridermal cells.
source: This exogenously added E-cadherin failed to rescue the smaller apical perimeter of the mutant peridermal cells. (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: aPKC regulates the polarised distribution of E-cadherin in the periderm via the cell polarity pathway and not by controlling the cell height or levels of E-cadherin.
source: These data confirmed that aPKC regulates the polarised distribution of E-cadherin in the periderm via the cell polarity pathway and not by controlling the cell height or levels of E-cadherin.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the rescue experiment results.

claim: A slight reduction in the E-cadherin intensities at various z-levels was found in both periderm and basal epidermis in pen/lgl2 mutant embryos at 72hpf.
source: We found a slight reduction in the E-cadherin intensities at various z-levels in both periderm and basal epidermis (Figure 3 A1, B1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: A slight increase in the peridermal cell-height and in basal cell-perimeter was observed in pen/lgl2 mutant embryos.
source: We also observed a slight increase in the peridermal cell-height and in basal cell-perimeter in pen/lgl2 mutant embryos (Figure 3 A2, B3; Mann Whitney U test, p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: There was no effect on polarised distribution of E-cadherin in pen/lgl2 mutants.
source: However, there was no effect on polarised distribution of E-cadherin in pen/lgl2 mutants (Figure 3 A4, B4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: has/apkc function is essential to maintain the robustness in adherens junction polarity along the apicobasal axis in the peridermal cells.
source: To conclude, has/apkc function is essential to maintain the robustness in adherens junction polarity along the apicobasal axis in the peridermal cells whereas pen/lgl2 function seems dispensable in this process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on has/apkc mutants.

claim: pen/lgl2 function seems dispensable in maintaining robustness in adherens junction polarity.
source: To conclude, has/apkc function is essential to maintain the robustness in adherens junction polarity along the apicobasal axis in the peridermal cells whereas pen/lgl2 function seems dispensable in this process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on pen/lgl2 mutants.

claim: E-cadherin is involved in homophilic adhesion.
source: E-cadherin is one of the crucial factors involved in epidermal cell adhesion (Tinkle et al., 2008; Tunggal et al., 2005). In the zebrafish bilayered epidermis, E-cadherin localises to the basolateral domain of the peridermal cells and to the apico-lateral domain of the basal epidermal cells. Since it is involved in homophilic adhesion, it is likely that lateral membrane localisation indicates adhesion between two neighbouring peridermal cells and two basal epidermal cells (Figure 1 A1, A2; Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The reduction of E-cadherin levels was not restricted to the peridermal clones, which received the morpholino, but was also seen in the underlying basal epidermal cells.
source: We observed that the reduction of E-cadherin levels was not restricted to the peridermal clones, which received the morpholino, but was also seen in the underlying basal epidermal cells. Of the 23 peridermal clones analysed, 19 clones showed a layer non-autonomous effect (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from clonal analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Of 44 basal epidermal clones analysed, 36 showed layer non-autonomous effect on membrane levels of E-cadherin in the periderm.
source: This was reciprocally true for the basal epidermal clones. Of 44 basal epidermal clones analysed, 36 showed layer non-autonomous effect on membrane levels of E-cadherin in the periderm (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from clonal analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The reduction in the levels of E-cadherin was not limited to the interface between the clone and underlying or overlying cells but was also observed at the lateral domains of the cells of the juxtaposed layer.
source: Most importantly, this reduction in the levels of E-cadherin was not limited to the interface between the clone and underlying or overlying cells but was also observed at the lateral domains of the cells of the juxtaposed layer (Figure 4A,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from clonal analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The clonal knockdown of e-cadherin resulted in a marked and statistically robust reduction in E-cadherin levels within the clone (CC) and at the cell-boundaries in the juxtaposed layer that completely overlapped (CO) with the clone.
source: This analysis confirmed that, whether in the periderm or basal epidermis, the clonal knockdown of e-cadherin resulted in a marked and statistically robust reduction in E-cadherin levels within the clone (CC) and at the cell-boundaries in the juxtaposed layer that completely overlapped (CO) with the clone.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of experimental data.

claim: The effect on the non clone-clone boundaries (NC) was moderate.
source: The effect on the non clone-clone boundaries (NC) was moderate.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of experimental data.

claim: The layer non-autonomous effect on the juxtaposed layer was stronger near the interface and decreased towards apical (in periderm) or basal (in basal epidermis).
source: It is also important to note that the layer non-autonomous effect on the juxtaposed layer was stronger near the interface and decreased towards apical (in periderm) or basal (in basal epidermis).
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The whole body knock down of e-cadherin function is lethal and the embryo does not develop past the epiboly stages.
source: As shown previously (Kane et al., 2005; Shimizu et al., 2005), the whole body knock down of e-cadherin function is lethal and the embryo does not develop past the epiboly stages.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Co-injecting e-cadherin mRNA along with morpholino rescued the early lethality phenotype.
source: Co-injecting e-cadherin mRNA along with morpholino rescued this early phenotype, proving the specificity of the morpholino used in this study (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Reduction in E-cadherin levels led to a decrease in membrane associated β-catenin, indicating a significant reduction in adherens junction formation.
source: Our analysis revealed that reduction in E-cadherin levels led to a decrease in membrane associated β-catenin, indicating a significant reduction in adherens junction formation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the morphant peridermal clones, aPKC was present basolaterally in the sub-cortical region, in addition to its apical localisation.
source: In the morphant peridermal clones, aPKC was present basolaterally in the sub-cortical region, in addition to its apical localisation (Figure 5A). Out of 18 clones analysed, 14 showed this effect.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Analysis did not reveal any effect on aPKC localisation in the periderm when e-cadherin was knocked down in basal epidermal cells.
source: Our analysis did not reveal any effect on aPKC localisation in the periderm when e-cadherin was knocked down in basal epidermal cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The loss of E-cadherin does not affect the apical domain in general but has a specific effect on aPKC.
source: We did not observe mislocalisation of ZO-1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), indicating that the loss of E-cadherin does not affect the apical domain in general but has a specific effect on aPKC.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ZO-1 localisation data.

claim: The knockdown of e-cadherin in either the peridermal or the basal epidermal clones showed an increase in Lgl2 levels.
source: The knockdown of e-cadherin in either the peridermal or the basal epidermal clones showed an increase in Lgl2 levels (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: E-cadherin deficiency in the periderm caused an increase in Lgl at the lateral membrane of the underlying basal epidermal cells.
source: In addition, E-cadherin deficiency in the periderm caused an increase in Lgl at the lateral membrane of the underlying basal epidermal cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: E-cadherin deficiency in the basal epidermis caused an increase in Lgl2 levels at the lateral domain of the juxtaposed peridermal cells.
source: Similarly, E-cadherin deficiency in the basal epidermis caused an increase in Lgl2 levels at the lateral domain of the juxtaposed peridermal cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Quantification confirmed a robust increase in Lgl2 levels in a layer autonomous as well as layer non autonomous manner.
source: Further quantification of the Lgl levels in clones that showed qualitative effect, confirmed a robust increase in Lgl2 levels in a layer autonomous as well as layer non autonomous manner. (Figure 5 B5, B6, C5, C6; Kruskal Wallis test with Dunn's post hoc test, significance values in Figure 5—source data 5).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Of the 19 clones expressing ΔEC1-EC2-Ecad version, 16 showed increased levels of Lgl2 in a layer autonomous as well as non-autonomous manner.
source: Interestingly, of the 19 clones expressing ΔEC1-EC2-Ecad version, 16 showed increased levels of Lgl2 in a layer autonomous as well as non-autonomous manner (Figure 5—figure supplement 4 A3, A5, B3, B5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: There was no detectable change in aPKC levels or localisation in clones expressing ΔEC1-EC2-Ecad.
source: However, there was no detectable change in aPKC levels or localisation in 15 such clones analysed (Figure 5—figure supplement 4 C3, C4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: The loss of e-cadherin function results in a loss of β-catenin localisation, suggesting a reduction in adherens junction formation.
source: To conclude, the loss of e-cadherin function results in a loss of β-catenin localisation, suggesting a reduction in adherens junction formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: E-cadherin restricts the localisation of aPKC to the apical domain in the periderm in a cell autonomous manner.
source: E-cadherin restricts the localisation of aPKC to the apical domain in the periderm in a cell autonomous manner, and controls the localisation of Lgl in a layer autonomous and non-autonomous manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: E-cadherin controls the localisation of Lgl in a layer autonomous and non-autonomous manner.
source: E-cadherin restricts the localisation of aPKC to the apical domain in the periderm in a cell autonomous manner, and controls the localisation of Lgl in a layer autonomous and non-autonomous manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Extracellular domains of E-cadherin play important role in controlling localisation of Lgl2 within and across the layers.
source: Our results suggest that extracellular domains of E-cadherin play important role in controlling localisation of Lgl2 within and across the layers.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ΔEC1-EC2-Ecad expression data.

claim: E-cadherin, by virtue of being a connector of the two layers, transduces polarity cues across the epithelium.
source: Thus, our data reveal that E-cadherin, by virtue of being a connector of the two layers, transduces polarity cues across the epithelium.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Adherens junctions are localised in a polarised manner in the zebrafish developing epidermis.
source: Here we have used zebrafish developing epidermis, a bilayered epithelium, as a model to show that adherens junctions are localised in a polarised manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: Peridermal cells show an increase in the level of E-cadherin and β-catenin from the apical to the basal domain.
source: Peridermal cells show an increase in the level of E-cadherin and β-catenin, and thus adherens junctions, from the apical to the basal domain whereas the basal epidermal cells show a reverse trend.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: The basal epidermal cells show a reverse trend in E-cadherin and β-catenin levels compared to peridermal cells.
source: Peridermal cells show an increase in the level of E-cadherin and β-catenin, and thus adherens junctions, from the apical to the basal domain whereas the basal epidermal cells show a reverse trend.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: The interface of the two layers has the maximum E-cadherin levels.
source: Thus, the interface of the two layers has the maximum E-cadherin levels.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the polarised distribution data.

claim: The two juxtaposed layers of the epithelium show reversed polarity with respect to the localisation of adherens junctions.
source: This is a unique system in which the two juxtaposed layers of the epithelium show reversed polarity with respect to the localisation of adherens junctions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: aPKC was not observed to localise in the apical domain of the basal epidermal cells during early development.
source: Consistent with this, we did not observe localisation of aPKC in the apical domain of the basal epidermal cells during early development.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

claim: The molecular identity of the histological apical domain of the basal epidermal cells remains undefined at the early stages of the epidermis development.
source: It appears that the molecular identity of the histological apical domain of the basal epidermal cells remains undefined at the early stages of the epidermis development.
evidence: This is speculation based on the absence of aPKC in basal epidermis.

claim: The basal epidermal cells may get the apical identity at the 'molecular' level possibly at a later stage when the polarity of the basal cells becomes important for the asymmetric cell division during stratification.
source: The basal epidermal cells may get the apical identity at the 'molecular' level possibly at a later stage when the polarity of the basal cells becomes important for the asymmetric cell division during stratification, as shown in mice (Helfrich et al., 2007; Niessen et al., 2013; Osada et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: aPKC controls the polarised E-cadherin localisation primarily via the polarity pathway.
source: Importantly, the decreased robustness in polarity is not a consequence of changes in the peridermal cell morphologies or E-cadherin levels, suggesting that aPKC controls the polarised E-cadherin localisation primarily via the polarity pathway.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the rescue experiment results.

claim: This is the first study to show a layer non-autonomous role of E-cadherin in a multi-layered epithelium.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to show a layer non-autonomous role of E-cadherin in a multi-layered epithelium.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: The disruption of adherens junctions leads to a loss of polarity and epithelial integrity in simple epithelia such as Drosophila blastoderm and follicular epithelium.
source: Earlier studies have shown that the disruption of adherens junctions leads to a loss of polarity and epithelial integrity in simple epithelia such as Drosophila blastoderm and follicular epithelium (Müller and Wieschaus, 1996; Tanentzapf et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A loss of e-cadherin function leads to mislocalisation of aPKC and improper formation of tight junctions in multi-layered epithelia.
source: In multi-layered epithelia, a loss of e-cadherin function leads to mislocalisation of aPKC and improper formation of tight junctions (Rübsam et al., 2017; Tunggal et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The weaker reduction in E-cadherin levels in the periderm upon e-cadherin knockdown in the basal epidermis may not be enough to mislocalise aPKC.
source: It is plausible that the weaker reduction in E-cadherin levels in the periderm upon e-cadherin knockdown in the basal epidermis may not be enough to mislocalise aPKC.
evidence: This is speculation to explain the lack of aPKC mislocalisation.

claim: The presence of maternally deposited E-cadherin protein facilitates the tight junction formation in EVL cells.
source: Presumably, the presence of maternally deposited E-cadherin protein facilitates the tight junction formation in EVL cells.
evidence: This is speculation to explain the lack of ZO-1 mislocalisation.

claim: The polarity of one layer is linked with the polarity of the neighbouring layer via E-cadherin.
source: Our Lgl data reveal that the polarity of one layer is linked with the polarity of the neighbouring layer via E-cadherin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Homophilic interaction dependent mechanism(s) may not play a role in regulation of Lgl2 localisation.
source: The fact that expression of EC1-EC2 domain deleted form of E-cadherin does not influence the E-cadherin localisation layer-non-autonomously but alters Lgl localisation in autonomous as well as non-autonomous manner, indicates that homophilic interaction dependent mechanism(s) may not play a role in regulation of Lgl2 localisation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ΔEC1-EC2-Ecad expression data.

claim: Tension mediated mechanism(s) might be contributing towards regulation of Lgl2 localisation.
source: It is therefore likely that additional tension mediated mechanism(s) (Borghi et al., 2012; Conway et al., 2017; Rübsam et al., 2017; Simões et al., 2010) might be contributing towards this regulation.
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The effect on Lgl2 and E-cadherin localisation away from E-cadherin deficient clonal boundaries can be explained via tension-based mechanisms.
source: The effect on Lgl2 and E-cadherin localisation away from E-cadherin deficient clonal boundaries can be explained via such tension-based mechanisms.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism.

claim: EVL cells are polarised along the apicobasal axis.
source: EVL cells are polarised along the apicobasal axis (Fukazawa et al., 2010; Lepage et al., 2014) and are likely to pass on this polarity to the peridermal cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: EVL cells are likely to pass on polarity to the peridermal cells.
source: EVL cells are polarised along the apicobasal axis (Fukazawa et al., 2010; Lepage et al., 2014) and are likely to pass on this polarity to the peridermal cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the developmental relationship between EVL and periderm.

claim: aPKC regulates the polarised localisation of E-cadherin in the periderm.
source: As the first step in our model (Figure 6), aPKC regulates the polarised localisation of E-cadherin in the periderm.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on experimental findings.

claim: The basal epidermal cells do not exhibit apical localisation of aPKC.
source: The basal epidermal cells do not exhibit apical localisation of aPKC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), consistently aPKC does not control polarity in the basal epidermal cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: aPKC does not control polarity in the basal epidermal cells.
source: The basal epidermal cells do not exhibit apical localisation of aPKC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), consistently aPKC does not control polarity in the basal epidermal cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the absence of aPKC in basal epidermis.

claim: E-cadherin begins to localise in the basal epidermal cells at 22 hpf.
source: During the early phase of epidermis development, E-cadherin begins to localise in the basal epidermal cells at 22 hpf (Arora and Sonawane, unpublished observations).
evidence: This is based on unpublished observations by the authors.

claim: The peridermal E-cadherin organises E-cadherin in the basal epidermis via homophilic interactions.
source: The peridermal E-cadherin- via homophilic interactions - organises E-cadherin in the basal epidermis.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on experimental findings.

claim: The higher levels of E-cadherin in the basal domain of the periderm allow greater localisation of E-cadherin in the apical domain of the juxtaposed basal cells, initiating polarity in the basal epidermis.
source: We propose that, as a consequence of homophilic interactions, the higher levels of E-cadherin in the basal domain of the periderm allow greater localisation of E-cadherin in the apical domain of the juxtaposed basal cells. Thus, initiating polarity in the basal epidermis.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on experimental findings.

claim: E-cadherin controls the levels of Lgl2 at the cortex, which is essential for the formation hemidesmosomes that mediate basal cells-to-matrix adhesion.
source: In addition, E-cadherin controls the levels of Lgl2 at the cortex (current analysis), which is essential for the formation hemidesmosomes that mediate basal cells-to-matrix adhesion (Sonawane et al., 2005; Sonawane et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by current experimental data and citations to previous literature.

claim: The results explain how E-cadherin and Lgl2 function antagonistically to regulate the hemidesmosome formation.
source: Our results presented here also explain how E-cadherin and Lgl2 function antagonistically to regulate the hemidesmosome formation (Sonawane et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings and previous literature.

claim: In the absence of aPKC function, the E-cadherin polarity is noisy but not completely lost, possibly due to existence of redundant mechanisms.
source: However, it is important to note that in the absence of aPKC function, the E-cadherin polarity is noisy but not completely lost, possibly due to existence of redundant mechanisms.
evidence: This is speculation to explain the partial phenotype in has/apkc mutants.

claim: A partially polarised periderm may still be able to transduce the polarity cues to the basal epidermis to set up the E-cadherin polarity.
source: Such a partially polarised periderm may still be able to transduce the polarity cues to the basal epidermis to set up the E-cadherin polarity.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism.
